utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. If there are no procedural matters, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the court room. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey has some re-examination for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rave. I first wanted to start off and ask you just a couple of questions about some of the OPs. There was quite a bit of questioning on cross about the OPs and the various motivations that may have been at play in dealing -- in the VRS's dealings with the OPs. So I first want to take you to something Major Franken testified about on 16/10/2006 on page 2460 of the transcript, and Mr. Thayer asked him: "On this day Private van Renssen was killed. Do you recall OP Foxtrot finally falling that day, sir?" And Mr. Franken answered: "Yeah, well, I already told that there was increased firings at the OP. It was hit several times. The defensive wall was blown away by tank fire so they asked permission to withdraw." Is that consistent with the reports or any information that you got.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same information that I've got, and at least they got the permission from the commander of the Bravo Company to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Franken goes on to say: "I gave that because the BiH was not inside anymore. They didn't inform us they were gone but they were gone. Then they waited for a pause in firing to withdraw, but it was too late. They were run over by Serb forces but were allowed to withdraw to Srebrenica." And is it when the crew of OP Foxtrot withdrew towards Srebrenica that van Renssen was killed by a Muslim fighter?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, not a Muslim fighter, a Muslim civilian who tried to stop the APC by returning to the road towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if that OP had not been assaulted like it was and the UN troop had not withdrawn, Renssen could very well be alive today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. For sure, because the BiH and also the civilians in the enclave did not allow us to go back, and, well, because they were attacked they had to go back. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I also wanted to ask you a couple of questions about OP Echo as were asked on cross-examination, especially on page 6788 through 6791 and 6836 by General Tolimir. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody. Just a clarification before Mr. McCloskey moves on to the second group of questions. Was he referring to P597 or the transcript, or actually is there a mistake in the transcript? Was he referring to anything that we heard in this case from this witness, i.e., the testimony of this witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you are talking about Franken's quote, I thought I said that. But in case I didn't, it was in trial here on 16 October 2006. Mr. Thayer's question was on 2459. The answer I read was 2460. And I think I probably didn't give you the page numbers, so that is -- to be clear that is the page number that those things were said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not in question. You were referring to these parts of the transcript in this case. Mr. Gajic, I must confess, I didn't quite understand your position yet, and the same seems to be the case for Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that things are clear. We are talking about P597, so we are not talking about the transcript of this case but the Popovic case transcript which has been admitted according to 92 ter. In 1996, we were not sitting, were we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is correct. That's more precise, though for the life of me the differences are beginning to get lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify the situation. Your quotation from a transcript was not the transcript of this trial but in Popovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is technically correct, but of course it is now a transcript of this trial, but I don't want you to think that he said that at this trial, that's correct, that's why I read the date out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have it clear on the transcript. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as I think I was saying, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about OP Echo because that was a significant part of the cross-examination. And I'd like to show you a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if I could get the usher to give you a hard copy. It's two pages and it might be easier for to you -- it's P625, if we could get that up in both languages, though I've also provided the Defence with two hard copies. They've got it in English and in B/C/S. This is a document that is already in evidence, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just study that, if you could. I won't take long with it, but as you are reading it, I'll just, for help -- the English will come up for the Court. And given that the Defence has hard copies of this, it might be easier if we blew up just in English on the screen so that it could be easier read. Okay. This is a document from the command of the Drina Corps from the forward command post at Pribicevac. And it's dated 2 June 1995. Can you remind us when OP Echo fell.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 2nd or the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this, if we go to the end of the document, we see that it's done by the commander Major-General Milenko Zivanovic and he was the commander of the Drina Corps at the time that you saw at the Hotel Fontana; correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And this is entitled: "Restoration of the control over the facilities and the Zeleni Jadar asphalt road." When it says, "facilities in Zeleni Jadar asphalt road," does that relate to any of the area that you talked about around OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when they are speaking about the facilities, they are speaking about the factory south of OP Echo and the road, that's the road on which OP Echo was stationed and which he ordered us to leave because they wanted to use the road as a line of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this is -- it's an order, as we see, and it's to the command of the Bratunac Brigade and to the commander of the Drina Corps Manoeuvre Battalion, and it says: "Considering from the military security aspect that the conditions have been created for the entry into the Zeleni Jadar industrial facilities down the road along the Jadar river, it is necessary, as soon as possible, to use the existing conditions and thereby enter the final phase of liberation of Zeleni Jadar in its entirety, so in that regard I hereby order ... on 3 June by 0500 hours he shall secure full combat readiness towards the enemy and the UNPROFOR check-point at his combat position." Is there any other OP check-point in Zeleni Jadar besides OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there only was the OP Echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't read everything. Talks about moving Legenda's troops and to monitor UNPROFOR. And then we see the paragraph: "Since Legenda and his troops shall allegedly search the terrain pretending not to see UNPROFOR, Petrovic's focal point shall be the behaviour of UN troops paying attention to the smallest change. When Legenda's troops receive warning from UNPROFOR to stop, Legenda shall inform UNPROFOR in English 'I am warning you: Do not stand in my way,' and according to his own assessment proceed towards UNPROFOR. If UNPROFOR points their weapons toward Legenda's troops, Petrovic shall fire warning Salvo and after that tell them in English: 'Hands up. Put down your weapons. ' If they do not comply with this order, fire a hand-held rocket launchers, Zolja, at the generator and be ready to neutralise the APC, paying attention not to hurt physically UNPROFOR soldiers." Do you know what he means when he says "generator"?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly what he means by generator. There might be a generator outside the OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right: "Petrovic shall vigilantly and intelligently monitor the situation and issue them an order, 'Hands up otherwise I'm not responsible for your lives.' At that time, Legenda's troops shall carefully approach the UNPROFOR position making sure that they are sheltered and physically far from UNPROFOR." This is the moment you can expect UNPROFOR to surrender. If UNPROFOR soldiers continue to reach out to their weapons in order to use it against Legenda, disable the APC with the hand-held rocket-launcher. That's the moment when one can expect UNPROFOR to surrender. On a signal that any of the UNPROFOR soldiers wish to surrender, Legenda shall inform them in English, and I quote: 'You are absolutely safe, my friends.' After that, Petrovic shall call Nikolic who will take UNPROFOR soldiers. Legenda and Petrovic shall take over the UNPROFOR check-point and after detailed discussion with Petrovic continue moving down the asphalt road and cross the Jadar in order to link up with the remaining part of the forces in the area of Kamenjara." Then there's another part of this order that I won't read. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this, what is laid out in here, it starts with pretending or I would say deceiving UNPROFOR, then it suggests that UNPROFOR be threatened, and then it suggests that if necessary assault UNPROFOR, then it suggests UNPROFOR will surrender and it says to then become friends with UNPROFOR. So this deception, threat, assault, surrender, befriend, does this sound familiar to you at all? Anything in your experience sound familiar in this document?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar, I think this is the way they acted, but in practice, of course, there was a little bit of different situation. In my memories they went to the OP Echo, started firing, threatened the OP and I don't know exactly how the fire fight was going on because I was not there, but I know there was a fire fight from UNPROFOR towards the attackers, I think. And at the end, the manning of the OP was able to get into the APC and not surrender but to withdraw and take -- try to take a new position a little bit farther up to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. There is also quite a bit of question about the Muslim people going towards Potocari or leaving the enclave. Did you ever happen to go in the spring of 1995 to the UNPROFOR garbage dump?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've been there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you see -- or when did you go?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I should take a look in my diary, I think. I don't know exactly when I was there. I know for sure I wrote something down. But I could find the date, if it's necessary. But it was a terrible situation over there. We had our garbage from the compound in Potocari, and once in awhile, a garbage truck-loaded with garbage and brought under the protection of the civilian police of the enclave towards the garbage dump. On the garbage dump most of the time there were a lot of people who knew that the garbage truck was coming over there and when the garbage truck was unloaded, the people tried to get into the garbage to find if there was something they could use either clothes, food, or anything, plastics and all those kind of things. Of course, it was a dangerous situation and the local police who had to protect the guys on the garbage truck and the unloading of the garbage truck started beating the local population to get them away for their own security, but it was a terrible view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just very simply, did the Serb forces restrict humanitarian aid to those people, the Muslims in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so because a lot of times only small UNHCR convoys came into the enclave so there was not enough food and not enough supplies for them to live in a normal humanitarian way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Mr. McCloskey. May these proceedings and in keeping with God's will and not necessarily according to mine. I don't think that that issue was raised in cross-examination. I don't object to Mr. McCloskey asking this question, but he is the one who insists on everything being done by the book, according to the rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you give us a reference to the relevant part in the cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it was constantly suggested in the cross-examination that the reason that the Muslim population was leaving was because they left on their own free will, perhaps to get away from the combat. That was said repeatedly throughout the cross-examination, and I'm merely showing this as another motivation aside from the -- what the General was putting forward in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am afraid, Mr. Tolimir, you didn't listen to the reasons given by Mr. McCloskey for his kind of question. But as you were not objecting, I would like to say please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You also said in cross-examination that at one point you went and spoke to General Mladic who was out amongst the crowd and General Mladic told you that these men would be taken to a POW camp near Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it was you were able to speak to General Mladic or communicate with him when you obviously don't speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was, of course, that our Muslim interpreters were too afraid to go out of the compound and being amongst the VRS soldiers in the vicinity of General Mladic, but most of the time the Colonel Jankovic was over there, he spoke English and Serbo-Croatian, so most of the time when I wanted to talk to General Mladic, I was able to use the Colonel Jankovic as an interpreter. So I used him as an interpreter to ask my questions to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in the specific situation that I asked you about, that you testified about this POWs going to Bijeljina, who was your specific memory of your translator, who was that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment it was Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General Tolimir also spent some time asking you about Camila Omanovic's brother and your claim that he talked about hanging himself. Did you receive any reports at that time of any Muslims hanging themselves in and around the area?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I've got one report about the Muslim man who hung himself in one of the factories in the night, I think, the night from the 12th to the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There was also General Tolimir, I think we'll all recall, asked you about the UN troops that were at the Hotel Fontana when you arrived there. Can you tell us when you and Colonel Karremans and Major Boering went back to your base in Potocari some 5 kilometres distance of Bratunac on that night of the 11th, did you take your troops with you?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed to take troops with us. They had to stay over there. We had the only possibilities after the 8.00 meeting just to see them for maybe five minutes, shake hands with all of them, wish them good luck and after that we had to leave the hotel and go back to our compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday during cross at page 6888, General Tolimir asked you this question in the context of talking about the Hotel Fontana meetings and your experience there: "I just want to ask the witness if he can remember any other threatening word from Mladic except his words, 'You can survive or disappear. Your fate is in your hands'?" Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't take the time to play the video the first meeting. But I just want to go back to some of the transcript references and that is at P01008 and ask you since you were there at that first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to go now to a section that is at page 20, roughly lines 20 to 25 in the English, and page 17, about line 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Mladic says to Colonel Karremans: "Does he smoke?" Interpreter says: "Do you smoke?" Colonel Karremans says: "Yeah, normally I do smoke, sir. Normally I do smoke, but I smoke so much that last days." Was Colonel Karremans a smoker?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he smoked. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Mladic: "Have a cigarette. This is not your last cigarette in life." Interpreter says to Karremans: "Light up. It's not your last one in this life." How did you take that comments as you were standing there listening to General Mladic say that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this fits in this the first ten minutes of this meeting because a lot of things were said in the same way, a lot of small threats going on, in my opinion, as well as the shouting towards me and to Mr. Boering that gave me the feeling in the first ten minutes that we could end up in the garden and be shot. So it fits in the whole scene at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let me go in the English to page 21, lines 1 through 12, and page 17, line 24 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans says: "I'd like to thank the Bosnian Serb military for treating my soldiers well." Interpreter says: "I'd like to thank the Serb military authorities for the good treatment of my soldiers." General Mladic says: "No need for that, thank you." Interpreter: "You don't need to thank." General Mladic now says: "They are here, in the hotel." Interpreter: "They are here at the hotel." Colonel Karremans says: "Okay, no problem." And General Mladic says: "But if you keep on bombing, they won't be hosts for a long time." And then the interpreter says: "If you keep bombing, they won't spend long time there." Did you hear Mladic say that that night?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall this specific sentence. But as I stated before, I think this fits in in the first ten minutes of the meeting in which a lot of those things were said and gave us the feeling not to be safe over there, and not having anything in our own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you take that to mean, that: "If you keep on bombing, they won't spend a long time there"? Who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was referring to our guys in the Hotel Fontana, but of course, he also threatened already, and I don't know if he did it before or after this statement, that if air-strikes were going on, he would also attack again or shell the compound, the refugees, and in this case also hurt our soldiers in the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to another section. Page 27 in the English, lines 22 to 34. Page 20 around line 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that on page 12, line 24, a wrong translation was recorded of the general's word at Fontana Hotel. It says here: "Keep on shelling. You won't be here for long," and I believe in the original it says: "You will not be host for a long time here," and the difference is huge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's very clear from the transcript that Mr. McCloskey were reading the sentence translated by the interpreter, but before we have on the transcript both versions, the original words in translation of General Mladic and later on the interpreter's version. There is a difference of course, but I think the quotation of Mr. McCloskey was absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And frankly, Mr. President, I don't see a big difference between the: They are not going to be hosted there anymore and they are not going to be there any more, I think it's pretty clear what General Mladic is talking about. Now, let me go, as I said to those previous pages, thank you for getting them up there and I'll start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it has been established what Mladic says because we can hear it. I believe that the record has to be corrected. We shouldn't rely on what the interpreter said, but rather we should rely on the original words of General Mladic. And the word that he used was "host" and I think for that reason our records should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I already said this was part -- the part Mr. McCloskey was reading. The whole text we could see in the transcript and we have seen this video several times so that everybody knows what was to be seen and to be heard in the transcript. Mr. McCloskey please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly so it's completely understood, this is a tricky situation in terms of translation, the reason of course that we put the Mladic version and the interpreter version is so that it's clear what the people at the Hotel Fontana would have heard because they don't understand General Mladic, so they are all important, what General Mladic actually said, what the interpreter said. So just to be made clear, that's why it's all laid out in this particular transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue. And at one point General Mladic says: "Are you married? Do you have a wife and children?" The interpreter says: "Are you marry the man, do you have wife and children?" Karremans says: "I have two children." Interpreter says: "I have two children." Was Colonel Karremans married at the time?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he was married, but I don't think that he had children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Mladic goes on to say: "How long have you not seen them?" Interpreter says: "For how long you haven't seen them?" Colonel Karremans: "For half a year." Interpreter: "Half a year." General Mladic: "And you would like to see them?" Interpreter says: "And you would like to?" Colonel Karremans says: "I beg your pardon?" Interpreter: "You would like to see them?" Colonel Karremans: "Oh yes, of course." How did you take it when General Mladic asked would you like to see your children?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, yes, in the same way as he did before, it was just a hidden threat that if you don't work together with us, if you don't act in the way I like to, your life is in danger. That was the feeling, at least I got, what I still feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. A couple more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 29 in the English, lines 23 through 29. Page 21 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Mladic: "Each of your officers and soldiers, just like yourself, has just one life." Interpreter: "Every one of you and your soldiers has only one life." General Mladic: "And I don't believe you want to lose it here." Interpreter: "And I do not believe that you would like to leave it here." General Mladic: "That's why I'm asking you to co-operate fully." Interpreter: "That's why I ask for absolute co-operation." How did you take that when he says: "And I don't believe you want to lose it here"?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when you read also the next sentence, it's quite clear. When you don't co-operate, it might be possible to lose your life over here and that's what we felt, at least what I felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, last one. Page 30 in the English, lines 24 through 33. Page 21 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Mladic says on the previous page: "I want to help you." Then on the page here the interpreter says: "I want to help you." And General Mladic says: "Although you don't deserve it." Interpreter says: "Even though you do not deserve it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey I'm not sure that we have that portion in B/C/S on the screen. It doesn't look very familiar to me but I'm not sure about that. Are these the correct pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see a reference to NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the English text we have only General Mladic and the interpreter. In the B/C/S version we have only General Mladic and later on Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we take a break, I'll fix that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No problem. You said page 30 in English and page 21 in B/C/S, perhaps it was not correctly recorded. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If that's page 21 in the B/C/S, it's my mistake. It shouldn't take us long to track it down. I apologise. It's the last one. Just a clarification while Ms. Stewart is looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you say the last one was a hidden threat as we have on the transcript or something else, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly recall, but I think it was a hidden threat because of course he was threatening us all the time, but in his words he made the show so that we felt it was a threat, of course, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he didn't actually threat us by saying, Well, I'll kill you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the mean time, I would like to note my observation that we have in e-court three times page 17 but in LiveNote only one page 17. In e-court page 17, lines 1 through 5, then again 17, 1 and 2, and then page 17 starting with line 1. I don't know what happened there but in LiveNote it's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. We won't take any more of the Court's time, it's in the record, we'll argue it. So I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The next witness should be brought in, please. Good morning, Mr. Thayer, welcome to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, it's nice to be back. Good morning, everyone. While the witness is being brought in, just for the Court's information, the next witness, his testimony is relevant to the following paragraphs of the indictment, if the Trial Chamber wishes to take a look. It's paragraph 21.14, and the Prosecution's pre-trial brief at paragraphs 115 to 116, just to provide a little bit of context. I know we jump around from topic to topic and this witness primarily addresses the events that occurred in these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Again, good morning, welcome to the courtroom. Please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution has questions for you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And welcome back. I think this is your third tour here in the Tribunal. Would you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Nebojsa Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall testifying over the course of two days in April 2007 in this courtroom in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you recently listen to all of your testimony in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did that audio recording accurately reflect your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, can you attest before this Trial Chamber if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked back in April of 2007, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P1280, the witness's Popovic testimony from April of 2007, as well as the following exhibits: P1283, P1284, and P1286 to P1300. There's one exhibit on the list which wasn't included in the 92 bis package, and I will address that exhibit with the witness shortly, and that's P1285.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, what about P1281 and 82?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Those are the transcripts, public and under seal version, respectively, of an additional day of testimony when Mr. Jeremic was brought back in the Popovic case as a Defence witness. My intention is to -- after I read the summary and should the Court accept the April 2007 testimony and the associated exhibits, to go through the same 92 ter procedure with respect to that Defence witness testimony and that will become an exhibit as well in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about P1285? You didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that is the exhibit that I referred to that was not included in the 92 bis package and I will address that during my supplemental questioning as well, Mr. President. That was the one gap in the list of be exhibits that I read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Another question, you are tendering P1298, 99, and P1300. They were not admitted in the Popovic case. I think you should consider to use them with the witness and tender them later because they are not part of the Popovic package.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER

I can tell you that with respect to P1298 and P1300, those were included on the list because they were used by Defence counsel during cross-examination of the witness in the Popovic case, they were quoted from by Defence counsel in the Popovic case, and in one case the witness, read to himself from his witness statement, which is P1298, so unfortunately nobody was -- is privy now to what he was reading, but for including it on the list. I can think of something, some reason to -- additional reason to show these documents to him in this proceeding, but, again, the reason why we included them in the 92 bis package to begin with, even though they were not admitted as exhibits in the prior trial because they were used with the witness in the prior trial, but for whatever reason Defence counsel didn't seek to admit them. But without them before the Trial Chamber, I'm afraid, as we've seen with other documents, you won't have an idea or fully accurate idea of what he is looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for much for this explanation. The Chamber will receive as exhibits, the exhibits number P1280, P1283 and 84, P1286 through P1297. The Chamber will postpone a decision about admission of the additional three documents we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President. I do have a summary for the witness. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The witness was born and raised in Zvornik and worked at the tax administration there as a lawyer. He was mobilised in May of 1992 as an infantryman, and in spring 1993 joined the service for combatting crime, which was part of the Zvornik Brigade's Military Police Company. The brigade's Military Police Company was commanded by Miomir Jasikovac, who in turn reported to the brigade's chief of security, Drago Nikolic. Nikolic was the witness's immediate superior for purposes of the service for combatting the crime, and Jasikovac was the witness's superior as regards any combat issues in the sphere of military police. The witness's office was located on the ground floor of the Bratunac Brigade's Standard Barracks in Karakaj. His unit dealt with criminal acts committed by brigade members; for example, murders, desertion, self-infliction of wounds and thefts. As part of their regular tasks, he and other two members of his unit Goran Bogdanovic, and Cedo Jovic, took statements from soldiers, wrote orders in the name of battalion commanders and the brigade commander Vinko Pandurevic, and wrote criminal reports and drafted charges. For example, they would write orders for Pandurevic for punishment up to 60 days in military prison for more serious offences. The brigade did not have to wait for approval from the military courts to impose such a sentence. Drago Nikolic would direct the witness's unit to draw up criminal charges and Nikolic would sign off on the charges. Because Nikolic was chief of security, the witness and his colleagues had to keep Nikolic informed of their progress. Each morning the unit would inform Nikolic of the situation in the military detention, after which Nikolic would report to Pandurevic for a daily morning briefing. Nikolic would then go to his own office and call the witness and his colleagues to hands down orders and instructions to them. On some of those occasions, when the witness reported to Nikolic's office, Jasikovac, the Military Police Company "komandir" was also there, receiving his daily instructions for his work from Nikolic. In Nikolic's absence, Nikolic's deputy, Milorad Trbic, would attend the daily briefing with Pandurevic, then pass on the orders and instructions to the witness and his colleagues. In the time-period immediately following the fall of Srebrenica, the witness spent his days and nights in the Standard Barracks, because there was an alert situation. At some point during this period, he saw buses of Muslim prisoners pass by Standard, driving in the direction of Bijeljina. The prisoners had their heads bowed and held their hands behind their necks and were guarded by Serb soldiers. Some unknown number of days after that, he heard rumours going around Standard that there were executions of Muslims in Orahovac and Pilica. Many people were talking about it. No one in the brigade requested the Military Prosecutor's Office to conduct investigation into these executions, and no one in his unit was ever instructed to conduct such an investigation. If such an investigation were ordered, that order would be come from Nikolic. The witness also testified about charges brought by the brigade against two brigade soldiers from the village of Lokanj; father and son Nesko and Slobodan Djokic. The chief of security Drago Nikolic told the witness that the two men had assisted the enemy, that criminal charges would be filed against them and that an order should be drafted for Pandurevic for 60 days' military imprisonment. The witness then interviewed the son Slobodan, who denied the charges until Nikolic came in and struck him, at which point the son said that his father had given four Muslim men some food and clothing and helped them reach the confrontation line to reach the other side. Bogdanovic then took statements from the father and son. Statements were also taken from the four Muslim men who had been assisted by the father and son and who were later captured, or who had been, I should say earlier captured, after their encounter with the father and son and were brought to Standard and held in the military detention there. The witness took three of those statements himself and Jovic took the fourth. The Muslim men were frightened, thin, and their clothes were in shreds. One of them said that he was from the village of Jagodnja in Bratunac municipality. Nikolic, Bogdanovic, and the witness then observed an identification procedure of the father and the son by the Muslim prisoners. The last time he recalls seeing the Muslim prisoners was in the office when they made their statements. He does not know how long they were kept at Standard or what happened to them. The statements of the father and son and four Muslims were taken between 23 and 26 July 1995. The witness went away on a work obligation for three months beginning on 26 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, has the summary been translated to you? Have you receive the final portion of the summary as I've read it out in translation?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is there anything that you would care to add or that I got wrong in the summary before we proceed?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The only thing that I would perhaps add is this: Statements were taken from Muslim prisoners as a future enclosure to the criminal report that would be written and then forwarded to the Military Prosecutor's Office. I think you skipped that in your summary and perhaps I should add it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. That's helpful, witness. Now, I want to ask you a few additional questions. Do you recall returning to testify again in this courtroom on the 23rd of September, 2008 as a Defence witness for the Drago Nikolic Defence?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you listen to that testimony as well recently?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you and I go over one error in the English transcript that was noted?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just read it into the record and we'll take care of that. This is at page 26102 of the 23 September 2008 transcript which has been marked at P1281, and this is in open session, so it's okay. This is at line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You had been asked the question: "To this day, you don't know where your fellow MPs were sent over this one, two or even three-day period; is that fair to say?" And you answered: "I didn't know at the time where they were. Now I do. I heard about that. However, while he was at the gate and around mid-July, I truly didn't know where the policemen had gone to." Now, is it fair to say, sir, in this last line that I just read where the English transcript reads: "However while he was at the gate around mid-July," it should read "while I was at the gate around mid-July"?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's fair to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now bearing that one correction in mind, sir, can you attest that the testimony which you listened to of your appearance in September of 2008 accurately reflects what you said?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can attest to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you further attest that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked in September of 2008, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P1281, the additional transcript, as well as P1282 which is the under seal version of that additional day of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's the other way around. 1281 is under seal, and 1282 is the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You are correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both documents will be received with these numbers. At this point in time, I would like to note that P1283 is a sketch with some B/C/S explanations. There's no English translation yet. I think it can only be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President, we'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you were born and raised in Zvornik and do you still live there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you are a Serb by ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the Standard Barracks are located in Karakaj. I'm not going to put you through map or sketch torture, but can you just generally describe for the Trial Chamber geographically where Karakaj is in relation to the town of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, the town of Zvornik is on the left bank of the Drina River and the Drina is the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbia. The Standard Barracks is located on the main road leading from Zvornik to Bijeljina. And according to my estimate, it is about 2 and a half to 3 kilometres away from the town of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say it's 2 to 3 kilometres away, can you tell us whether it's 2 to 3 kilometres to the north, south, east, or west of the town of Zvornik along that road leading to Bijeljina? If you can't remember that's okay. I think the Trial Chamber has been there recently. We don't want you to guess, so if you just don't remember, that's okay, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the side of the world. We over there don't talk in those terms. We never mention east, west, south, or north. I only know that it is on the left bank of the -- about 3 kilometres from Zvornik on the main road leading from Zvornik to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember is Karakaj between the town of Zvornik and Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think that does it for us, thank you, sir. And the Standard Barracks themselves, prior to the war what kind of facility was that building, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I remember before the war it was a shoe factory. That's where shoes were made. That was a new building of the shoe factory facility. I am talking about the period before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during your testimony in the Popovic case, you made references to both the chief of security Drago Nikolic, as well as his deputy, Milorad Trbic. In the Standard command building, where did they have their offices, if you recall? And did they have separate offices or did they share an office? Sorry to give you two questions in one, but ...

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I understand, that's okay. The office of chief of security Drago Nikolic was on the first floor at the main entrance, and he shared his office with his second in command, Milorad Trbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again without putting you through sketch torture, can you tell the Trial Chamber where in relation to Commander Pandurevic's office, the chief of security's office was located? Just where in relation to each other, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Drago Nikolic's office was on the first floor at the main entrance, as I've already told you. And that's where the brigade commander Vinko Pandurevic's office was as well. The only difference being that the commander's office was at the far end of the corridor, and a bit before that office on the left-hand side, there was Drago Nikolic's office. In other words, both the offices were located on the same floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in your experience as a member of the Zvornik Brigade, who in the Zvornik Brigade was responsible for escorting and guarding VRS soldiers who were being held in detention for these crimes that you testified about you were in charge of investigating?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The military police were in charge of that, the Military Police Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who in the Zvornik Brigade was responsible for escorting and guarding any prisoners of war who were brought to or detained at the Standard command?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: When it comes to POWs who were kept at the Standard, the military police were in charge of them as well, and I'm talking about those who were kept at the Standard building.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: And that also applied to VRS troops who were kept in custody at the Standard building. Again, the military police were in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I want to take you through a couple of documents. And these mostly pertain to the charges that were brought against this father and son, Nesko and Slobodan Djokic, for helping these four Muslims who were trying to reach the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd first like to show you P1299, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would just take a moment and re-familiarise yourself with this document and I'll ask you a couple of questions. Just let us know when you are ready to go to the next page, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Now is the time to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we'll need to -- in the B/C/S there will be a blank page next and then we'll need to go to the page after that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. You can start putting your questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. My first question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can go to the second page of the English for this first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a signature there in -- underneath the Cyrillic name, do you recognise that signature and whose signature is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I recognise the signature. It is Goran Bogdanovic's signature. We worked together in the office to prevent crime at the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go back to the first page in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You testified in the Popovic case that you were present for the interview of the son, Slobodan Djokic; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you also testified that on or about the 26th of July, 1995, you left the Standard command to begin a work obligation elsewhere; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you have any specific recollection of being present when this particular statement was taken by Mr. Bogdanovic from the son, Slobodan Djokic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that I was there when the son, Slobodan Djokic, and his father Nesko were brought in. And when my colleague Goran was taking this statement from them, I can't remember, actually, but I was there when Slobodan Djokic was interviewed. I don't know when the statement was taken and signed. I can't remember. I only know that I was present during the interview with Slobodan who spoke about those things, and he admitted during that interview that he had, indeed, wanted to help Muslim soldiers. And as for this statement and when it was typed up, I don't know. I can see that it was Goran Bogdanovic who took the statement and signed it. I wasn't there but I was there during the interview, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your review of this statement taken by Mr. Bogdanovic, how does it compare with your recollection of what the son, Slobodan Djokic, told you when you were present during the interview with him?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The statement and the interview pretty much tally. I think that everything that is indicated in the statement is true and correct because I, myself, interviewed Slobodan about the events and all that, all that he stated during his interview was then typed up and presented as a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just one last question regarding this document before the break. If we look at the first paragraph that begins right under the date of 26 July 1995, I just noted that it refers to Slobodan Djokic, son of Nesko and mother Andjelka, born 1 December 1971 in Donji Likanj, Zvornik municipality. Based on your familiarity with this case, is this village, the name of this village here typed accurately, Likanj, or is it a different name?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The name of the village is Donji Lokanj, L-o-k-a-n-j.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time the Prosecution would tender P1299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'm about to go on to another document, so perhaps this is a good time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We must have our first break now and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have P1291 on e-court very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what we have here is a statement taken from Sakib Kiviric, and it's dated the 23rd of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could just advance two pages in the B/C/S to the last page of the document, and the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature there, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So if we could go back to the first page in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think you testified about this statement in the Popovic case. This individual, Sakib Kiviric, is one of the four Muslims who were brought to the Standard command and from whom you personally took the statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to note a couple of things very quickly before we move on to the next statement. It indicates here that he was born on the 24th of June, 1964, in Jagodnja, municipality of Bratunac, and that he is a conscript, a member of the 283rd Eastern-Bosnian Light Brigade. So he has identified himself as a soldier, has he not?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could look at P1292, very quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Same exercise, very quickly. We have here a statement of Emin Mustafic, dated 23 July, 1995. He identifies himself as being a conscript member of the 280th Eastern-Bosnian Light Brigade, born 7 October 1969. Do you see that, sir, in the very top of the document?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just go to the last page, which is the third page in B/C/S and the second page of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, do you recognise the signature there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: My signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. May we have P1293, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Here we have a statement of Fuad Djozic, dated 26 July 1995, born 2 May 1965, driver my profession, a member of the 280th Mountain Brigade as driver. If we could go to -- do you see that, sir, first, before we move on?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the third page in B/C/S and again the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature there, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cedo Jovic, that's my third colleague. There were three of us in the crime prevention service of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think in your testimony before the break, you referred to these four Muslim men as soldiers, and clearly they've identified themselves in their statements, anyway, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could look at P1294, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have here a statement of Almir Halilovic, dated the 23rd of July, 1995, son of Suljo and Dika, born 25 August 1980, in the village of Bajranovici, municipality of Srebrenica. You see that there at the top, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, if we could just go to the third page in B/C/S, second page in the English, just to see who took this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature there, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we can just go again back again to the first page in each version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The date of birth here, 25 August 1980 indicates that Almir Halilovic would have been just shy of his 15th birthday at the time he was brought to the Standard command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And his young age probably explains why there's no indication that he is a member of any military unit; is that fair to say, based on your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: You could say that. He certainly did not say himself that he was a member of any military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I know it's going back over 15 years now, sir, but do you have any recollection as you sit here today at all in your mind's eye of this boy? And if you don't, that's okay, I'm just testing your memory a little bit to see if you do have any recollection of this boy.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P1290, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the Popovic trial, you were asked a number of questions about this document. We'll talk about it a little bit more in a moment, but you were asked a number of questions about this document which is a ruling ordering detention for three days for the father and son. And you also testified about Drago Nikolic instructing you and your colleagues to draw up an order for Vinko Pandurevic's signature, Pandurevic being the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, for 60 days' military imprisonment. So my question for you is: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber the relationship, as you understood it, between this three day detention and the 60 day military imprisonment? Did the three days cancel out the 60 days or supersede it, or were they to be served one after the other, if you know? Can you help the Trial Chamber by clarifying that issue just a little bit, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, this ruling remanding Nesko Djokic and Slobodan Djokic in custody for three days does not cancel out the order of the brigade commander that we were told to write stipulating 60 days in military prison. I did not write this ruling, but I think it was written in order to be attached to the criminal report, in order to remand them in custody for three days, the time it takes to follow the procedure, take statements from them, do an identification and collect all the other evidence in order to send them to the Military Prosecution's Office along with a criminal report. I believe that's why this ruling was written, although I didn't write it myself. And this ruling did not change the order of the brigade commander. The order of the brigade commander to put them in military prison for 60 days remained in force, but I don't know if it was written. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That was very clear, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have P1295, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I was told that the last document, P1290 is in B/C/S a 20-page document. The English translation consists only of two pages. You used only that part which has a translation. What about the remaining pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is an explanation, Mr. President. And that is, when these documents were seised, there were multiple copies in the original versions of the same document stapled together or attached. If you look at the original document, it is literally, and this is the case with the other statements that we just went through, in the files as the OTP investigators found them, there were multiple copies of the documents, virtual, identical, mimeograph, or however they were copied, they were copied and just stapled together. So rather than retranslating each version, only the first copy was translated. That's why there's the difference in page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To have the record clear, I think we should only admit the first two pages in B/C/S as well. If the other pages are only copies, there's no reason for admission of these documents. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would respectfully disagree that that suggestion, Mr. President, makes eminent common sense. Unfortunately, common sense sometimes isn't the most efficient guide in these cases. The documents have already been uploaded in full. If the Court wishes simply to admit those first three pages of the document and then choose to ignore everything else, then I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I want to stop you. I'm persuaded. I think it's the best way to leave it like it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, you'll also have noted that there are blank -- or what appear to be blank pages interspersed and that's just how we found these document, so those got an evidence stamp as well. With the Court's permission, I have a couple of more documents to use with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremic, do you see before you the statement of Nesko Djokic, taken on 25 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. It indicates that he was born on the 1st of January, 1936 in Donji Lokanj, Zvornik municipality; do you see that there, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at the statement, it begins on 18 July, 1995: "I got up early in the morning to bring grass for my cattle from a field which is about 150 metres from the house. On my way there, four men appeared before me under an apple tree. I knew immediately that they were Muslims, since they were covered with blood and also by their clothes, because they had been fleeing from Srebrenica towards their territory at that time." And I think just to save some time, there's no dispute that this statement was taken by Goran Bogdanovic on this date. My question for you, sir, is: You described in the Popovic trial the clothes that they were wearing as being in shreds and that they were thin and they looked frightened. By the time that they arrived at the Standard command on or about the 23rd of July, do you recall any blood being on their clothes or on their bodies?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I did not notice that they were bloodied. I said already they were exhausted, fearful, their clothes were torn, but I didn't notice any blood on them. Perhaps a few minor scratches, but I don't remember any serious injuries or wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. That was my next question, sir. So did you observe that they had required or received any medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember that they received any medical attention. I made them tea, if that counts as attention, but as for sending them to the infirmary that was available in the brigade, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So it's fair to say from what you recall, you didn't see any injuries or wounds on these four individuals?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I didn't see any serious injuries. For instance, that someone was bleeding or that they had a fracture on any part of the body. I don't think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we move to P1184, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what we have here is a report dated the 26th of July, from the security organ of the Zvornik Brigade command to the military prosecutor in Bijeljina, and the heading of the report is "Collaboration With the Enemy" You've seen this document before, I don't think there's any mystery about that, you saw it in the Popovic case and reviewed it during your proofing; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the third page in B/C/S and the second page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on this page, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I do. It's the signature of Drago Nikolic, chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just noticed this morning what I believe is a translation error, maybe you can help clarify this for us. In the original B/C/S right next to the signature page there is a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just blow up that stamp so it's a little easier for Mr. Jeremic to read, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can read what that stamp says, looks like "vojna" something. Can you read that into the record and tell us what those words mean there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The stamp says military PO box. I think the number is 7469, Zvornik. That's the number of the military PO box. It's a bit smudged but I think the number is 7469, military PO box, Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And that, to your recollection, belongs to the Zvornik Brigade as a whole? When you say that that is the military post or PO box, you are referring to the brigade itself; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Because I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify, are you referring to the right side of this stamp offer the words on the left side?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The words on the left side in Cyrillic where it begins with a letter that looks like B-o-j-h-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that that is "vojna," that word there, and the next word is "posta"?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's "vojna posta" written in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Because it's been translated incorrectly as stamp of the military police and what is the word in your language for military police, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: "Vojna pilicia," there's no other word for police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, that was just a little correction I wanted to go through with you on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to clarify that. "Posta" is not the same word as police are, could you clarify that please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremic, in your language what does the word "posta" mean?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: "Posta" is an institution that receives and sends letters, telegrams, and parcels. It's post, "posta," in our language. Has nothing to do with the military police. How shall I explain it? The post receives parcels, letters, telephone communications, and communicates these further to addressees, that's a civilian institution post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So in your experience, sir, did each brigade have a different military post number? You said here it's listed as 7469, so in your experience, for example, would the Romanija Brigade, or some other military unit like a brigade or a corps have a separate post office or post number assigned to it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I didn't come across the numbers of any other military post. I believe that every brigade has its own military post number. I really wouldn't be able to tell you that. I'm not a military professional, but it would only be logical for each brigade to have a different post number. And now why the term "military post" is used for that, I really don't know. You should ask somebody else who is a career soldier who would be able to explain that better than me. I don't know why it is called a military post and whether each brigade had its own number. Our brigade number was what I told you and I suppose that the other brigades had other numbers. I really can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I add one last question. Did Mr. Drago Nikolic use this stamp usually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I believe that P1184 has been provisionally admitted through the testimony of Kathryn Barr, so I am not sure if it's technically in sort of the MFI netherworld as a result. If it is, I would take the opportunity to tender this exhibit P1184 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, there were a couple of documents that were shown to you during the last trial but that weren't offered by the parties that used them during the last trial into evidence. So I want to go over a couple of matters with you regarding another one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is P1298, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What we have here is a copy of your statement to the OTP taken on 12 January 2006. And if we look at the English version, do you see your signature anywhere on that first page in the English version on the right, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And prior to signing the English version, sir, do you recall that the statement was read to you by an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was read to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of the English. I think that's going to be page 6 of the B/C/S. We'll be looking at paragraph 17 in any event. Great, we got it. Sorry, page 5, for the record, for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the Popovic trial, this is at transcript page 10445 to 10446, one of the Defence attorneys asked you to read your statement. He actually quoted to you from the statement, and in particular I want to focus on paragraph 17. So if you could just take a moment and read that to yourself.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The beginning of the paragraph states: "After this investigation, the prisoners were returned to the detention room at the brigade. I knew that the prisoners remained there for a time as I used to walk down that passage on occasion. Some days later, I noticed that the prisoners were no longer there. I do not know what had happened to the prisoners and have never received any official explanation as to what became of them." My first question, sir, is: This portion of paragraph 17 refers to which particular prisoners, just so there's no confusion in the record?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It refers to the Muslim prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The four Muslim prisoners who were assisted by Nesko and Slobodan Djokic, sir, is that -- just to put a finer point on it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I believe that the first three or four sentences do refer to the four Muslim prisoners, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. This paragraph goes on. You say: "In my opinion, the brigade commander or the chief of security were the ones who made the decisions about the prisoners." Can you just -- you don't need to go into any great detail about this, sir, but can you share with the Trial Chamber upon what experience is your opinion based that the brigade commander, Vinko Pandurevic, or the chief of security, Drago Nikolic, were the ones who made the decisions about the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I said here that that was my opinion, which doesn't really mean that -- I mean, since the detention unit was under the control of the military police and that the military police were in charge of the detention unit and the chief of security was the one making decisions in respect of the military police, I think that he was also responsible for all the detainees who were taken by the Zvornik Brigade, including the Muslim prisoners. That's my opinion, although he never issued orders either to me or to my service with regard to the Muslim prisoners. The only exception being our task to take the statements from those four who had been brought in. And since the brigade commander was superior to the chief, I concluded that he also made decisions about that. That's simply my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Now, do you recall whether there were any occasions when members of the Military Police Company failed to discharge their duties properly and were removed from the company as a result? And we don't need particular names. You don't need to put anybody's particular name on the record. I'm just asking you if you recall such occasions.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I think that some were indeed removed. I don't know why, whether they breached the military discipline. In any case, it was not that they refused to carry out an order. It was always a matter of breach of discipline of some other kind and for those reasons such policemen would be removed from the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall which officer in the brigade took that action to dismiss those members?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The chief of security who was also responsible for the military police, he was the one who dismissed military policemen from the company and it was most often as a result of their behaviour and a breach of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue in this paragraph 17. You say: "I was not at any meetings where the fate of the prisoners were discussed." And then, and this is what I believe the Defence counsel in the Popovic trial was directing your attention to: "I do recall at one stage, soldiers from the Bijeljina Brigade arriving in trucks to transport between 80 and 100 Muslim prisoners away. Some of these prisoners were wounded. Someone mentioned that they were being transported to Batkovici prison, although I never received any confirmation that this was the case. I cannot recall if the prisoners I took statements from were transported with these trucks or were taken away separately." First question is: Do you stand by what is contained here in the statement paragraph 17 that I just read out? Is that accurate? Does that reflect your recollection of events?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, what I stated is accurate, but I would like to add something else. I'm not sure that those were soldiers from Bijeljina. The information that I had was not really accurate. There were just rumours. Or soldiers said that they were being transferred to Batkovic and Batkovic is close to Bijeljina, and that's why I concluded that they originally came from Bijeljina, from one of the brigades over there. That was just my conclusion. I'm not sure about the exact name of the brigade that took them away. That was just my conclusion. Otherwise, I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you provide any further detail in terms of the date when this occurred, and let's just start with the fall of the Srebrenica enclave as one marker in your mind? Can you help the Trial Chamber at all approximately when you recall these soldiers arriving to take these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that that happened after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. A long column of Muslims was moving from Srebrenica in the direction of Tuzla on foot. There were civilians and armed fighters among them. I didn't see the column myself, but I heard it from those who did see it, and many got lost on the way. There was fighting, the column split. Some crossed the line, some didn't, some stayed behind and wandered around.
